title: Framed: Astonishing True Stories of Wrongful Convictions
author: Robert F. (Bob) Cromie
target_audience: General public concerned with miscarriages of justice
Educators or researchers studying wrongful convictions
core_themes: Wrongful convictions and miscarriages of justice
Limitations and errors in the legal system
The impact of bias, sloppy police work, and flawed forensic evidence
Consequences for victims, families, and society
The role of media and public opinion
primary_purpose: To illuminate real instances of wrongful convictions, shed light on the human and systemic factors behind them, and raise awareness about the complexities and fallibility of the criminal justice system.

structure_format.organization: Collection of individual case studies, each recounting a wrongful conviction
features: Analysis of investigative and legal errors
Personal perspectives of the accused and affected parties
Occasional commentary connecting cases to broader justice system issues

key_concepts_lessons: Miscarriages of justice can happen to anyone, often due to systemic flaws.
Mistaken identity, false confessions, forensic errors, and misconduct are frequent causes of wrongful convictions.
Once a wrongful conviction occurs, overturning it is extremely difficult and often takes years.
The consequences of wrongful imprisonment are profound, affecting lives, families, and public trust.
Systemic safeguards (like appeals and DNA testing) are crucial but not always effective or available.
notable_features: Draws from a wide range of real-life cases, some famous and others less well-known
Vivid narrative prose contextualizing legal details in accessible terms
Highlights repeated patterns and root causes of wrongful convictions
Emphasizes the human toll as well as larger social implications
cultural_historical_context: The book was released amid rising awareness about flaws in the criminal justice system in North America, including the Innocence Movement and advances in forensic technology. It contributes to ongoing dialogue about criminal justice reform and public skepticism about infallibility of law enforcement.
reception_impact: Appreciated by true crime readers for its compelling, meticulously researched cases
Draws attention of criminal justice reform advocates and legal professionals
Praised for storytelling and clear explanation of legal concepts
Critics may argue that such narratives can foster excessive distrust in law enforcement if not contextualized
comparable_titles: Actual Innocence by Barry Scheck, Peter Neufeld, Jim Dwyer
The Innocent Man by John Grisham
Picking Cotton by Jennifer Thompson-Cannino and Ronald Cotton
